column4: The houses are permitted أَن تُرْفَعَ, God's name is remembered in them, and He is glorified there; one setting unites the section's raising, name, remembrance, and tasbih.
The believing magicians tell Pharaoh لَن نُّؤْثِرَكَ, refusing the very act of preference used for choosing the low life in 87:16; their refusal begins the sequence that ends in the highest degrees.
Within the magicians' reply, وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ states the same better-and-more-lasting judgment as 87:17 and explains why they will not prefer Pharaoh in 20:72.
The criminal in Hell لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ exactly restages 87:13; here it stands immediately before the believers' high degrees.
The believer who comes with good works receives ٱلدَّرَجَٰتُ ٱلْعُلَىٰ, turning height from Pharaoh's claim into an awarded rank and completing the contrast with 20:74.
The gardens are called the reward of مَن تَزَكَّىٰ, completing the 20:72-76 sequence with the purification that precedes remembered prayer in 87:14-15.
Pharaoh says أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ; a creature seizes both “Lord” and “Most High,” staging the section's corrupted elevation.
The judgment begins with مَن طَغَىٰ, naming the transgression embodied by Pharaoh's claim in 79:24 and preparing the low-life choice in the next ayah.
وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا exactly joins preference to the low/near life, as in 87:16, and identifies the choice beneath counterfeit height.
Hell becomes the refuge of the one who transgressed and preferred the low life in 79:37-38, supplying the consequence corresponding to 87:12.
Fearing the station before the Lord and restraining desire reverses 79:37-38: true regard for the Lord checks the self that chooses the nearer life.
The Garden is the refuge of the one described in 79:40, completing the opposite outcome to Hell in 79:39.
God tells the fearful Moses إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ; superiority is granted in the very confrontation where Pharaoh falsely claims the title for himself.
فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ repeats the section's command, Lord, name, and glorification while replacing “Most High” with “Magnificent.”
The surah closes by repeating فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ, making glorification through the Lord's name the response to its final certainties.
فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ is the same command-frame as 87:1 and again makes the named Lord, rather than a creature, the bearer of greatness.
The purified giver seeks only وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ; “Most High” names the Lord as the enduring object chosen over recompense or possession.
وَرَفَعْنَا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ states the section's dictionary relation literally: remembrance or renown is raised.
The revelation descends from the creator of ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ ٱلْعُلَى, locating creaturely height in heavens made by the Lord called Most High.
The revelation-bearer is described as ذُو مِرَّةٍۢ and standing poised; this gives the figure whose appearance on the high horizon follows in 53:7.
وَهُوَ بِٱلْأُفُقِ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ realizes the dictionary image of a figure becoming distinct at the high horizon.
فَتَعَٰلَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱلْحَقُّ gives true kingship and exaltation to God, directly answering the section's account of a king who “rose” by tyranny.
ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ joins the Lord's name to the command and to creation, as 87:1-2 joins glorifying the name to the Creator.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ is the direct counterpart of remembering the Lord's name in 87:15 and makes that remembrance an undivided turning to Him.
تَبَٰرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ ذِى ٱلْجَلَٰلِ وَٱلْإِكْرَامِ makes the Lord's name itself the locus of blessing, majesty, and honor.
وَرَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ is the Quranic act named by the section's dictionary note on takbir: ascribe greatness to the Lord.
وَكَبِّرْهُ تَكْبِيرًۢا commands unqualified magnification of God after denying Him child, partner, and protecting patron, giving tesbih's content through takbir.
وَلِتُكَبِّرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمْ makes magnifying God the response to His guidance, joining the section's greatness-language to the guidance of 87:3.
لِتُكَبِّرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمْ locates greatness in thankful worship rather than in the sacrificial bodies or human possession.
وَلَذِكْرُ ٱللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ explicitly calls God's remembrance “greater,” joining the section's two lexical claims about dhikr and greatness.
وَلَهُ ٱلْكِبْرِيَآءُ فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ assigns الكبرياء throughout creation to God, setting the rightful possession of greatness against human pretension.
سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ وَتَعَٰلَىٰ ... عُلُوًّۭا كَبِيرًۭا combines transcendence, elevation, and greatness while clearing God of what people say, almost a lexical summary of the section.
God alone is ٱلْمُتَكَبِّرُ and سُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ clears Him of partners; the ayah distinguishes divine greatness from the blameworthy greatness creatures assume.
The Creator has ٱلْأَسْمَآءُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ and everything glorifies Him, directly bringing creation, names, and tasbih together.
God makes the disbelievers' word ٱلسُّفْلَىٰ and His own word ٱلْعُلْيَا; the section's high-low axis becomes a judgment between rival claims.
إِنَّ فِرْعَوْنَ عَلَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ uses the exact corrupted sense developed in the prose: a ruler “rises” in the land by tyranny and division.
إِلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ ٱلْكَلِمُ ٱلطَّيِّبُ makes good speech ascend to God and righteous action raise it, giving a vertical scene for elevated name and remembrance.
The Prophet says فَتَعَالَيْنَ to wives who desire ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَزِينَتَهَا; the “come” form derived from height stands inside the same low-life choice.
Choosing God, His Messenger, and the final home reverses the choice of worldly life in 33:28 and makes explicit what stands at the upper end of that decision.
أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِى directly binds remembrance of the speaking Lord to prayer, the same pair joined in 87:15.
Trade and sale do not distract these people from God's remembrance and prayer; their conduct in the raised houses of 24:36 reverses preference for the low life.
The call to prayer requires hastening to ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ and leaving trade, staging remembered worship against immediate worldly gain.
People leave the Messenger standing for trade or amusement, but مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌۭ; the scene exposes the low-life preference that 62:9 had interrupted.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ commands remembrance of the Lord's name, matching the wording and stance of 87:15.
Prostration and long glorification at night enact the worship commanded in 76:25, joining remembrance of the name to bodily lowering before the exalted Lord.
ٱذْكُرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ذِكْرًۭا كَثِيرًۭا makes abundant remembrance the believers' commanded stance.
وَسَبِّحُوهُ completes the command of 33:41 by pairing remembrance with glorification, the same two motions joined across 87:1 and 87:15.
Remembering the Lord much and glorifying Him morning and evening places dhikr and tasbih in one divine instruction.
The final home is assigned to those who do not desire عُلُوًّۭا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ; renouncing self-elevation becomes the way to the enduring higher outcome.
The coming event is خَافِضَةٌۭ رَّافِعَةٌۭ, lowering and raising; it turns the section's lexical axis into an eschatological reversal of rank.
ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْأَدْنَىٰ is set below ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْأَكْبَرِ, placing “nearer/lower” and “greater” at opposite ends of one punitive scale.
The hereafter is أَكْبَرُ دَرَجَٰتٍۢ وَأَكْبَرُ تَفْضِيلًۭا; the low-life choice is corrected by greater ranks and greater preference beyond it.
The flower of worldly life is a test, while وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ repeats the better-and-more-lasting counterweight to 87:16.
Worldly provision is temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ, explicitly decoding why the nearer life is lower.
What people receive is only enjoyment of worldly life, while what is with God is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ for believers.
Worldly life is rain-fed vegetation that becomes scattered dry matter; it gives the passing low life the same pasture-to-refuse trajectory present in Surah 87's context.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, but enduring good deeds are better with the Lord and better in hope, completing the passing scene in 18:45.
Worldly life is play, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in increase, then vegetation that dries and becomes debris; apparent greatness ends in disappearance.
أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ asks whether people are satisfied with the low life in exchange for the hereafter and calls its enjoyment little.
They preferred ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا عَلَى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ, an exact statement of the section's choice with its proper object of comparison.
Those who love worldly life over the hereafter also obstruct God's way, showing the directional consequence of preferring what is near.
بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ restates preference for the nearer life without using دنيا: they love what comes immediately.
وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ names what is abandoned when the immediate is loved in 75:20.
They love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ and leave a weighty day behind them, another nonlexical formulation of choosing nearness over the final horizon.
They purchase worldly life with the hereafter, turning the section's preference into an exchange and exposing the low value of what they buy.
مَتَٰعُ ٱلدُّنْيَا قَلِيلٌۭ وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ declares the worldly enjoyment little and the hereafter better, directly interpreting the high-low valuation.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while the final abode is better for the God-fearing; fear redirects value away from the low life.
Those satisfied and at ease with worldly life ignore God's signs; contentment with nearness is presented as the decisive misvaluation.
Fire is the refuge earned by the people described in 10:7, joining satisfaction with the low life to the fire-end named in the section.
Whoever desires worldly life and its adornment may be paid fully in it, making the chosen near horizon explicit.
Those confined to the desire in 11:15 have nothing in the hereafter but Fire; the distant consequence exposes the low value of the fulfilled near desire.
Expanded or measured provision belongs to God, and worldly life compared with the hereafter is only an enjoyment; provision and valuation meet in one claim.
Whoever wants ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ receives only what God wills and then Hell, binding preference for immediacy to its limit and outcome.
Whoever wants the hereafter and strives for it in faith has the striving appreciated, giving the opposite orientation to 17:18.
God extends His gift to both groups, showing that present provision does not by itself certify the height of either choice.
Worldly life is diversion and play, whereas the final abode is ٱلْحَيَوَانُ, the true life; the “low life” is denied final claim even to fullness of life.
Worldly life is a temporary enjoyment, while the hereafter is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the lasting home.
Gold and worldly luxury are reduced to mere enjoyment, while the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
People exhaust their good things in worldly life and act arrogantly on earth; humiliating punishment joins the low-life choice to counterfeit elevation.
وَلَلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكَ مِنَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ states the same better-later valuation without using دنيا, sharpening the temporal dimension of low/near.
The armies occupy ٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا and ٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلْقُصْوَىٰ, using the root in its concrete “nearer bank” sense and displaying the spatial axis behind الدنيا.
The Romans are defeated فِىٓ أَدْنَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, a concrete nearest/lower land use that preserves the spatial sense behind “the low/near life.”
ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا means the nearest heaven; الدنيا here marks nearness within an explicitly elevated cosmic scene rather than worldly life.
وَزَيَّنَّا ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا again uses الدنيا for the nearest heaven, separating the root's spatial nearness from its moral valuation of life.
ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا is adorned with lamps, placing the “nearest” term in a luminous heaven and exposing the root sense beneath worldly usage.
ثُمَّ دَنَا فَتَدَلَّىٰ follows the figure at the highest horizon with drawing near and descending; height and nearness become movements in one vision.
أَوْ أَدْنَىٰ measures an even nearer distance, completing the motion from the high horizon rather than treating “near” as low in worth.
وَٱسْجُدْ وَٱقْتَرِب joins bodily lowering in prostration to true nearness, a concrete reversal of seeking elevation for oneself.
God teaches Adam ٱلْأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا; names make the created things knowable, directly illustrating the dictionary account of a name as what identifies an essence.
Adam discloses the beings' names while God declares knowledge of the heavens' and earth's unseen, linking naming as disclosure to what remains hidden.
The supposed gods are only names coined by people and their fathers without divine authority; bare naming fails to raise a nonexistent referent into lordship.
The most beautiful names belong to God and are the means by which He is called; deviation in those names is condemned, guarding rightful naming.
The objects worshipped besides God are only names invented by people, while judgment belongs to God alone; the ayah separates labels from true lordship.
After naming Him Lord of the heavens and earth and commanding worship, the ayah asks whether any سَمِيّ can be known for Him, protecting the uniqueness of the divine name.
ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ لَهُ ٱلْأَسْمَآءُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ locates all beautiful names in the sole deity whose exaltation frames the surah.
The idols are only names coined by people and their fathers without authority, another boundary between a raised sound and a real divine referent.
Calling “Allah” or “the Merciful” reaches the same one to whom the beautiful names belong, making names disclose rather than divide their bearer.
The revealed book contains ذِكْرُكُمْ, plausibly both reminder and honored mention; this activates the section's secondary sense of dhikr as distinction.
وَإِنَّهُۥ لَذِكْرٌۭ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ explicitly makes revelation a remembrance or honor for the Prophet and his people, matching dhikr's elevated secondary sense.
وَرَفَعْنَٰهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا says Idris was raised to a high station, a literal realization of honorable mention becoming elevation.
وَٱذْكُرْ فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِدْرِيسَ gives Idris remembered mention immediately before God raises him high in 19:57.
God grants Abraham's family لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّۭا, a lofty truthful renown that realizes the section's link between mention and height.
Abraham asks for لِسَانَ صِدْقٍۢ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرِينَ, a truthful later renown; it supplies the prayer behind the lofty mention granted in 19:50.
God asks Iblis أَسْتَكْبَرْتَ أَمْ كُنتَ مِنَ ٱلْعَالِينَ; assumed greatness and imagined membership among “the high” are exposed as refusal to bow.
Pharaoh's people reject signs ظُلْمًۭا وَعُلُوًّۭا despite inner certainty, defining their elevation as willful injustice rather than superior truth.
Pharaoh is لَعَالٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ and among the extravagant, another contextual use of “high” for oppressive worldly ascendancy.
Pharaoh and his chiefs act arrogantly and are قَوْمًا عَالِينَ, showing collective self-elevation in the Moses confrontation.
Pharaoh is called عَالِيًۭا مِّنَ ٱلْمُسْرِفِينَ as Israel is delivered from his humiliating punishment, joining height-claim to excess.
The children of Israel are foretold to rise عُلُوًّۭا كَبِيرًۭا through corruption, combining the section's height and greatness roots in a blameworthy form.
Those who seek greatness on earth without right are turned from God's signs, showing how self-elevation blocks the reminder that could raise them rightly.
Those disputing God's signs harbor only كِبْرٌۭ مَّا هُم بِبَٰلِغِيهِ, a greatness they will never attain; the ayah states the failure inside their upward claim.
The arrogant walker cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height, measuring human self-exaltation against physical limits it cannot cross.
Pharaoh orders a tower fired from clay so that he might climb toward Moses' God; false lordship turns elevation and fire into a manufactured challenge.
Pharaoh asks Haman for a lofty structure so he may reach the routes, staging political greatness as an attempted ascent.
The requested routes lead toward the heavens so Pharaoh can look at Moses' God, but his scheme only bars him from the way; literal ascent exposes spiritual lowness.
Pharaoh proclaims his Egyptian dominion and visible rivers, using assembled worldly spectacle to support the superiority claimed in 79:24.
Pharaoh calls Moses مَهِينٌ and scarcely articulate, pushing his rival downward in the same speech by which he elevates himself.
Abraham sees the moon بَازِغًۭا and then setting; the crescent or orb emerging at the horizon becomes a test of whether visible height deserves lordship.
The rising sun is called هَٰذَآ أَكْبَرُ, yet its setting disproves its lordship; apparent celestial greatness is measured against the enduring Lord.
After the setting lights, Abraham turns to the creator of the heavens and earth, transferring devotion from high visible forms to their Maker.
Abraham answers a ruler's claim over life and death by challenging him to bring the sun from the west; a creature's sovereignty fails at the horizon.
The divine light parable contains a lamp kindled from a blessed tree and culminates in نُّورٌ عَلَىٰ نُورٍۢ; it supplies the light-fire majesty immediately before raised houses in 24:36.
At the fire seen by Moses, the call blesses what is in and around it and says سُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, bringing fire, manifested splendor, and tasbih into one scene.
Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring news or a burning brand; this establishes the distant fire whose divine call and tasbih occur in 27:8.
Moses sees a fire and hopes to find a brand or guidance at it; the same fire becomes the place where the Lord commands remembered prayer in 20:14.
Moses perceives a fire from the mountain and approaches for news or a brand, staging light seen at a distance before the divine naming in 28:30.
From the fire-side tree Moses hears إِنِّىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ رَبُّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ; the luminous scene discloses the true Lord by name.
When divine manifestation crushes the mountain, Moses falls and wakes saying سُبْحَٰنَكَ; creaturely height collapses before the splendor to which tasbih responds.
A blazing fire is announced just before the purified giver is kept from it and seeks the face of his Most High Lord in 92:17-20.
The most God-fearing is kept away from the blazing fire of 92:14, preparing the purification and Most High Lord of the following ayat.
The giver spends wealth يَتَزَكَّىٰ, joining purification to the movement toward the Most High Lord named in 92:20.
The warned fire is called إِحْدَى ٱلْكُبَرِ, one of the greatest things, giving the fire's greatness root an explicitly eschatological referent.
The Throne encompasses heavens and earth and God is ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ; cosmic rule joins true elevation to magnificence.
God knows hidden and manifest and is ٱلْكَبِيرُ ٱلْمُتَعَالِ, uniting greatness with transcendence rather than with an earthly claim.
Those without faith receive the evil description, while God has ٱلْمَثَلُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ; the highest description is reserved for Him.
Because God is the Truth and rival invocations are false, He is ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْكَبِيرُ; height and greatness follow exclusive lordship.
فَتَعَٰلَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱلْحَقُّ repeats 20:114's true King formula and follows the denial that creation was purposeless.
The highest description belongs to God in heavens and earth, and He is mighty and wise; divine height governs both realms.
The contrast between God as Truth and false objects of invocation ends with وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْكَبِيرُ.
After intercession is stripped from creatures except by permission, the divine speech is affirmed as truth and God as ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْكَبِيرُ.
Those who believed when God alone was invoked but disbelieved when partners were named are judged by ٱللَّهِ ٱلْعَلِىِّ ٱلْكَبِيرِ.
Ownership of heaven and earth belongs to God, وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ; the title rests on possession rather than assertion.
The heavens nearly rupture from above while angels glorify their Lord, turning the divine height of 42:4 into cosmic tasbih.
The domestic warning closes إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّۭا كَبِيرًۭا, placing every exercise of human authority beneath God's height and greatness.
وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ ties being uppermost to faith and steadiness after defeat, paralleling the divinely granted superiority of Moses.
وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ وَٱللَّهُ مَعَكُمْ grounds the believers' upper hand in God's presence, not self-magnification.
God يَرْفَعِ believers and people of knowledge دَرَجَٰتٍۢ, showing elevation as a divine award joined to faith and understanding.
رَفِيعُ ٱلدَّرَجَٰتِ ذُو ٱلْعَرْشِ names God as high or raiser of degrees and possessor of the Throne, the source of every true rank.
God gives and removes rule and grants honor or humiliation as He wills; the two-direction movement denies rulers ownership of their height.
God raises the heavens without visible pillars and settles over the Throne, assigning literal cosmic elevation to the Creator.
وَٱلسَّمَآءَ رَفَعَهَا and the setting of the balance make height a created order rather than a boast.
رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّىٰهَا describes God raising and proportioning heaven shortly after Pharaoh's false “Most High” claim in the same surah.
The hearer is asked to look at the sky كَيْفَ رُفِعَتْ, directing attention from visible height to the act of its raising.
The oath by ٱلسَّقْفِ ٱلْمَرْفُوعِ presents heaven as a raised roof, a creaturely height that points beyond itself.
Humanity is returned أَسْفَلَ سَٰفِلِينَ after creation in the best form, a stark downward reversal that makes moral height contingent.
The record of the righteous is in عِلِّيِّينَ, an explicitly high register contrasted with the wicked record in Sijjin.
The question وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا عِلِّيُّونَ marks the high register as a reality needing disclosure, not a self-claimed rank.
A written register defines what Illiyyun contains, giving content to the high designation introduced in 83:18.
Those brought near witness the high register, joining true nearness to the righteous height of 83:18.
After people invent partners and children for God, سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ وَتَعَٰلَىٰ clears and exalts Him above their descriptions, precisely enacting the prose's definition of tasbih.
God is declared glorified and exalted above the intercessors people associate with Him; transcendence removes a false heavenly hierarchy.
سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ وَتَعَٰلَىٰ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ begins the surah by combining glorification and exaltation against association.
The denial of a son or rival god ends سُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ, making tasbih the clearing of the true Lord from creaturely descriptions.
Creation and choice belong to the Lord, then سُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ وَتَعَٰلَىٰ removes the partners people elevate.
سُبْحَٰنَ رَبِّكَ رَبِّ ٱلْعِزَّةِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ states explicitly that glorifying the Lord means clearing Him of their descriptions.
After measuring all creation within God's grasp, سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ وَتَعَٰلَىٰ clears Him above partners and exposes their failure to estimate His true greatness.
The Lord of heavens, earth, and Throne is glorified above what they describe, joining cosmic height to transcendence from false speech.
The imagined plurality of gods would ruin heaven and earth, so the Lord of the Throne is glorified above their descriptions.
The claim that the Merciful has taken a child is answered سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ; the alleged children are instead honored servants, separating divine transcendence from granted honor.
The Prophet announces his clear path of calling to God and says وَسُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ, joining missionary stance to clearing God of association.
تَعَالَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ كَلِمَةٍۢ سَوَآءٍ calls people upward, in the dictionary history of تعال, toward a common word that no one take another as lords.
تَعَالَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ وَإِلَى ٱلرَّسُولِ is an upward-form call toward revelation, while hypocrites turn decisively away.
The call تَعَالَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ is refused for inherited ancestral ways, staging the etymological upward invitation against settled human custom.
تَعَالَوْا۟ أَتْلُ مَا حَرَّمَ رَبُّكُمْ uses the height-derived invitation to summon hearers toward the Lord's concrete moral boundaries.
When told تَعَالَوْا۟ يَسْتَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ, hypocrites turn their heads in pride; they refuse an upward-form call because of self-elevation.
تَعَالَوْا۟ قَٰتِلُوا۟ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ summons the hypocrites into costly duty, but their retreat reveals the distance between verbal nearness and moral ascent.

تَعَالَوْا۟ نَدْعُ أَبْنَآءَنَا uses the dictionary's “come up” form for a summons to a decisive mutual invocation; the lexical history supplies the vertical undertone, though the ayah does not state height.
The moon is measured through phases until it returns like an old palm stalk; its changing visible crescent supplies the celestial form used in the section's sumūw dictionary image.
The ayah treats crescent forms as time-signs; it activates the section's dictionary picture of the hilal becoming distinct above the horizon, though the ayah itself does not describe its rising.
وَٱلْقُرْءَانِ ذِى ٱلذِّكْرِ may carry honor as well as reminder, so it plausibly reflects the section's secondary “dhikr as distinction” sense, but the semantic choice is not explicit here.
